# Discussion

## Outcomes

The PCA and K-means clustering results suggest that data centers are not evenly distributed across the contiguous United States. Instead, they appear to be strongly associated with key county characteristics, especially larger populations and greater land area. This is reflected in the large difference in the average number of data centers between the two clusters, with Cluster 0 averaging about 1 data center and Cluster 1 averaging about 10, even though the PCA model only used population and county land area, and county water area. Because cluster 0 captures more rural county characteristics while Cluster 1 aligns more closely with urban counties, these findings challenge the common assumption that data centers are primarily built in remote, open areas. Instead, our results suggest that data centers are often located in more urban settings. This may partly reflect our broad definition of data centers, which likely includes smaller urban deployments in addition to larger campus-style facilities.

The difference-in-differences results indicate that data center presence is associated with mixed economic outcomes rather than a uniformly positive or negative effect. On the negative side, data center presence is linked to declines in personal income and in certain sector-specific employment measures, particularly trade and transportation, industrial, and primary industry employment. On the positive side, data center presence is associated with lower unemployment, increased construction activity, and lower air pollution. Taken together, these results suggest that data centers may bring real local benefits, but these benefits must be weighed against the potential economic costs and tradeoffs that also appear to accompany them.

We also explored a variational autoencoder to look for additional non-linear relationships between data centers and the outcome variables, but the model did not produce any clearly interpretable results. While it was a useful exploratory approach, it did not contribute meaningfully to the core findings of the project.

## Ethics

As noted in our data sources, all of our data come from government sources and are aggregated at the county level. Because of this, no personally identifiable information is used in the project, so there are no major personal privacy concerns.

One potential source of bias is that, although we use many data sources, there may still be important underlying county characteristics that are not captured in our data. For example, demographic trends or population composition may influence both where data centers are located and the economic outcomes we measure. Because we include limited demographic information, this could introduce omitted variable bias, which may cause some of our estimated relationships to reflect unobserved differences rather than the direct effect of data centers themselves. For this reason, our project is framed around associations rather than causal claims.

Another important ethical consideration is that economic data are not just abstract numbers, they represent real effects on people’s livelihoods. For example, an increase in unemployment reflects real job loss and can have serious consequences for individuals and communities. We have tried to reflect this throughout the project by using careful language and avoiding exaggerated or dismissive interpretations of the results. Any conclusions drawn from this work should acknowledge those real-world impacts.

## Limitations & Future Work

The biggest limitation of this project is the lack of consistent publicly-available data on data centers. Many private data sources are behind substantial paywalls, while some public sources do not provide historical or time-based information, and others use definitions of data centers that are inconsistent or difficult to verify. For that reason, we used the NAICS 518 definition of data centers, which gave us a consistent, government-defined measure that is reported regularly by QCEW and makes the project easier to replicate. The tradeoff is that NAICS 518 is broader than true data centers alone, so it may include some facilities or businesses that are not actually data centers. For example, it may capture firms that provide related computing or web-hosting services but are not operating large-scale data center infrastructure.

A second major limitation is that our spatial measures are only approximations. Because counties do not operate in isolation, we tried to capture regional spillovers by using nearby cluster estimations. While this gives a useful regional signal, it is still a simplification and may be less accurate in areas where counties are very large, very far apart, or geographically heterogeneous. Our 50 mile buffer approach for nearby data centers was another way of approximating spatial effects, but because we did not have exact facility locations, we had to assume data centers were evenly distributed within each county. That assumption is imperfect and makes the nearby-data-center estimates harder to interpret.

Future work would benefit most from a public dataset that includes all of: a consistent data center definition, exact facility locations, dates of operation, and size or scale measures. That would make it possible to separate large data center campuses from smaller related facilities and would improve both treatment measurement and spatial analysis. Future work could also expand the environmental side of the project by revisiting water use and land use impacts, which we were not able to model reliably because of data availability issues. In addition, the exploratory modern machine learning work we began with the variational autoencoder could be extended further to test whether more complex non-linear relationships exist between data centers and local economic outcomes.
